title: Eli Lilly CEO Reveals One‑Third of New GLP‑1 Users Choose Foundayo as Production Surges
body:
Eli Lilly’s chief executive, Dave Ricks, told a CNBC interview on Monday that roughly one‑third of patients newly prescribed a GLP‑1 oral therapy are now taking the company’s brand‑name tablet, Foundayo. The disclosure comes as the pharmaceutical giant accelerates manufacturing capacity to close the gap with Novo Nordisk, which currently dominates the burgeoning market for once‑daily, pill‑form glucagon‑like peptide‑1 (GLP‑1) drugs used to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity.

Foundayo, Lilly’s first oral GLP‑1 candidate, received FDA approval in early 2024 after a series of late‑stage trials demonstrated comparable efficacy to injectable counterparts while offering the convenience of a daily tablet. Since its launch, the drug has been positioned as a “bridge” for patients reluctant to begin injectable therapy, a segment that represents a sizable share of the roughly 34 million Americans living with type 2 diabetes. Ricks’ comment that a third of new GLP‑1 pill users are already on Foundayo suggests that the product is gaining traction faster than many analysts had anticipated.

The market dynamics, however, remain heavily skewed toward Novo Nordisk, whose oral GLP‑1 agent, Rybelsus, entered the United States in 2019 and has since amassed a substantial share of prescriptions. Novo’s early entry allowed it to lock in relationships with insurers, clinicians, and pharmacy benefit managers, creating a high barrier for later entrants. Lilly, which historically excelled in injectable GLP‑1s such as Trulicity, has been forced to pivot quickly to an oral format to remain competitive in a space that is now expanding beyond diabetes to address obesity—a condition with an estimated 100 million adults in the United States alone.

To meet rising demand, Lilly announced a multi‑phase expansion of its production lines at facilities in Indiana and Ireland, targeting a 50 percent increase in output by the end of 2025. The company also disclosed plans to invest $1.2 billion in next‑generation oral delivery technology, aiming to improve bioavailability and reduce dosing frequency. These moves are intended not only to satisfy current demand but also to position Lilly for future product launches, including a pipeline of oral GLP‑1 analogues currently in Phase III trials.

Industry observers note that the surge in oral GLP‑1 prescriptions reflects broader trends in patient preference and payer policies that favor non‑injectable therapies. “The convenience factor cannot be overstated,” said Karen Liu, a senior analyst at HealthEquity Research. “Physicians are more likely to initiate therapy when the barrier to adherence is lower, and insurers are increasingly rewarding oral agents with better formulary placement.” Nonetheless, price sensitivity remains a critical factor; Lilly’s Foundayo is priced slightly above Rybelsus, prompting some payers to negotiate rebates or favor the incumbent.

Looking ahead, the competitive landscape is set to intensify as other major drugmakers, including Pfizer and Merck, disclose their own oral GLP‑1 programs. Lilly’s ability to sustain its momentum will hinge on scaling production without compromising quality, securing favorable reimbursement terms, and demonstrating real‑world outcomes that match or exceed those of its rivals. If the current uptake trajectory holds, Foundayo could secure a meaningful share of a market projected to exceed $30 billion globally by 2030, reshaping the therapeutic approach to diabetes and obesity and cementing Eli Lilly’s role as a key player in the next generation of metabolic medicines.
